speechtext:
I wish to say but a very few words in support of this bill. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) and I have not always agreed on many matters, but I say to him now that the introduction of this bill does credit to his humanitarian instincts. I support the bill for two distinct reasons. In the first place I think this amendment should be given careful and serious consideration; as a matter of fact, it should be accepted, because we should not have on the statute books a provision that merely to become a public charge under the conditions that prevail in the country to-day shall be considered a crime. At least it should not be classed among the other reasons that are set out in the section under which a person may be deported, that he has had to apply for relief. May I, for the benefit of hon. gentlemen, who possibly may not be acquainted with it, read section 40 of chapter 93 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927. That section reads:
Whenever any person, other than a Canadian citizen or person having Canadian domicile, shall be found an inmate of or connected with the management of a house of prostitution or practising prostitution, or who shall receive, share in, or derive benefit from any part of the earnings of any prostitute or who manages or is employed by, in, or in connection with any house of prostitution or music or dance hall or other place of amusement or resort habitually frequented by prostitutes, or where prostitutes gather, or who in any way assists any prostitute or protects or promises to protect from arrest any prostitute or who shall import or attempt to import any person for the purpose of prostitution or for any other immoral purpose, or who has been convicted of a criminal offence in Canada or who admits the commission prior to landing or entry to Canada, of a crime involving moral turpitude, or has become a professional beggar or a public charge . . .
That is, who loses his job and has to appeal to the authorities for relief. In this section, such a person is classed with the others who are enumerated in the first part of the section. There are a number of other persons mentioned in this section who may be deported, but I do not believe that becoming a public charge, in the sense that a person has to apply for relief, should be considered a cause for deportation in Canada.
I support the amendment also because of the conditions that exist in many parts of
Europe to-day. We know there are a great many people who because of race or because of their political opinions find conditions in their own country intolerable. For instance, we know that in Germany people of the Jewish race are persecuted and driven out of the country; but there is another class of people in Germany who are persecuted, and who as a matter of fact are in a worse position than the Jews because they cannot leave the country. I refer to the Social Democrats. The Jew can make his case known, and if it is known that he is a Jew every effort is made to get rid of him; but the Social Democrat cannot admit that he is a Social Democrat because he would be immediately subjected to persecution. Because of that fact, he cannot make application to leave the country. So he has not the opportunity to leave.
There are people in Canada who have been here three or four or five years and who may be socialists in their political opinions. If we deport such people because they have become public charges, in the sense that they have applied for relief, we are sending them back, as the hon. member says, to certain death or at any rate to spend the rest of their lives in concentration camps.
For these reasons I submit that the amendment should 'be accepted. I do not agree with the position taken by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid). We allow people to come into Canada, and to me it makes no difference whether they are white, yellow, black or 'brown, we should not discriminate against them. They have been allowed to come in under the laws of Canada, and while here, through their productive efforts, they have added to the wealth of the country. We should not in any way discriminate against such people because their skins may be yellow and their eyes slanted. We shall have to raise our moral concepts a little higher than that and get away from some of our racial prejudices if we are to hold our place in a world that can be called civilized.
I hope that the government will consider this amendment favourably and take the necessary steps to make it law.

I recall cases where the officials-I am speaking now of the senior officials in the department- have recommended deportation-sometimes they make no recommendation-and I have not accepted their recommendation because on examination of the evidence I did not think deportation warranted. I quite admit the position of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni that the law as it stands may impose a hardship upon a person who is charged with being on relief. But I say that since I have had anything to do with this matter-I speak only of my own observation-that is pretty effectively guarded against at the present time.
The proposed amendment suggests further that such a person who may otherwise be subject to deportation, if he makes representations to the board of inquiry that deportation would be likely to place him in a position where he would suffer trial and punishment, or punishment without trial, in the country to which he would be deported, can claim the right to have this taken into account by the board of inquiry. The amendment would impose upon the board of inquiry the necessity of conducting an investigation into such an allegation.

speechtext:
Precisely. What does that mean? A person who comes before a board of inquiry on the ground that he lias become a public charge says, "I do not want to be deported because if I am sent back to Germany or Austria or Russia or some other country I shall be sent to a concentration camp or tried for some offence and my life may be endangered." Under this provision, as I read it, it would be necessary to have such a complaint or assertion inquired into and investigated before deportation could take place. That would impose upon the board of inquiry a duty which I do not think it would be practicable for it to discharge. Consequently I think it would make the administration of the law in that regard very difficult.
I quite admit the contention of my hon. friend that occasion may arise of hardship of the kind described being imposed upon some individual by a deportation order. But while that may arise, I can say to the house quite frankly that I do not think it has resulted in any of the cases that have come to my attention. Let me make it clear, Mr. Speaker, that I am not speaking of any previous administration, because I do not know anything about any other administration. I do say, however, of my own knowledge that when deportation orders have been issued there have been occasions when the board issuing the order has recommended that it should not be put into effect. There have been cases in which the officers more immediately on the spot have made such recommendations; there have been occasions when, after these matters came to the notice of the senior officials of the department, as in due course they must, they have made such recommendations and, when none of these things happened, there have been cases that have come to me in which I have allowed the appeal.
Under those conditions I think I should say to the house that the administration of this act at the present time is carefully guarded to avoid inflicting upon any person charged with being on relief the penalties theoretically provided by the law. I may say further that I considered bringing in some other amendments to the act, because some clarification is required in one or two respects in connection with this matter of deportation so far as provincial laws are concerned; but it was decided to let the matter stand over until next year, when it is the intention of the department to bring in some amendments to the act. I do not know how far my hon. friend wishes to press his amendment. I believe in its present form it would be difficult to accept, because I am afraid that any complaints which might be made by a person to the effect that he would suffer serious penalty if deported could not usually be investigated. So I would suggest to my hon. friend, and I would be glad to have him give the matter consideration, that the point in his amendment that I believe has some merit might well stand over until another session when, if I have anything to do with the administration of the department, I shall be glad to see that it is included in the amendments submitted.

subtopic: BEAM TRAWLING-AMENDMENT RESPECTING VESSELS TO BE REGISTERED AND BUILT IN CANADA

speechtext:
Mr. J. J. KINLEY (Queens-Lunenburg) moved the second reading of Bill No. 37, to amend the Fisheries Act, 1932.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill purports to make a short amendment to subsection 2 of section 56 of the Fisheries Act, 1932. Under section 56 it is provided that every person shall be guilty of an offence and shall incur a penalty who attempts to fish or to cause any other person to fish with otter trawls or similar equipment, except under licence from the minister, and in order to qualify for such licence at the present time such vessel must be registered as a British ship in Canada and be owned by a Canadian. The present amendment would change this qualification to read "unless such vessel has been built in Canada and is registered as a British ship in Canada and is owned by a Canadian."
The bill does not decide the question of the merits whereby a licence is granted, but it does make a difference in what vessels can apply for a licence to the further extent that they must be built in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, it is nearly nine o'clock, and I should like to see the bill receive consideration and perhaps go to a committee. I know the minister from Nova Scotia is interested in it, and it may be that he would want to make an announcement to the effect that we could send the bill to a committee. Perhaps that would be the best thing to do, because it is a matter of detail. I suggest the bill is important and a matter worthy of the consideration of the house, especially of the fisheries committee. Therefore, as the hour has almost expired I shall not say anything further at this stage, but will, in order to advance the bill to-night, ask that it be sent to the fisheries committee.

I say that condition is not fair to the fishermen of Nova Scotia. Before I sit down may I say that I appreciate the attitude the minister has taken that he does not wish to have this purchasing board cluttered up with small contracts. speechtext:
I think the $5,000 limit was arrived at largely by analogy to other matters. As my hon. friend knows, under the Public Works Act any contract of over $5,000 is subject to the procedure of calling for public tender. Under regulation of, if I am not mistaken, the treasury board the same thing applies, that all contracts of over $5,000 must be submitted to council. But that is because $5,000 is considered to be a fairly reasonable amount.
Perhaps if we went to the genesis of the legislation we would conclude that it arises out of the desire of the minister and the government and the house generally to avoid any criticism of what are known as munition contracts. I do not suppose anybody in the house desires that the ordinary administration of the department should be in any way interfered with. The objections are with respect to munition contracts. I can hardly conceive of any objectionable munition contract which would be under $5,000. What is in the mind of the public at this time and in the minds, I think, of all of us, is to prevent what is called war profiteering, profiteering in blood. We have heard it often enough on the hustings and in this house. It seems to me that the bill goes pretty far when it states that this board, which, after all, is a board to deal with munition contracts, shall have full power and authority to inquire into these. Heaven knows, it will have work enough. Does any hon. member suggest that a contract for clearing snow at the citadel at Halifax or at Quebec, the sort of contract which is called for in the ordinary course of business of the department, and represents under $5,000, probably $1,500 or $1,300 for the whole *winter, should be submitted to the special board? It is dealt with without even going to council; no order in council is called for in these cases.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CREATION OP DEFENCE PURCHASING BOARD TO ENTER INTO CONTRACTS FOR MUNITIONS, EQUIPMENT, MATERIALS AND SUPPLIES

The other day when this subject came up in another connection, the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan), if I remember rightly, expressed the hope that when the defence purchasing bill came before the house, no effort would be made to have any transfer from the Department of National Defence to the finance department. He said that a move of the kind would be in the nature of a departure from the principle of ministerial responsibility. I do not agree with that view. I do not think there is any departure from responsible government in having financial matters referred to a treasury board, but I do think there is something still owing to ministers of the crown, who are heads of different departments, that they should all to as great an extent as possible be treated alike with respect to the administration of the affairs of their several departments. I would certainty look upon a request to transfer every contract, no matter how small the amount might be, over $100 and up to the figure named here, from the Department of National Defence to the Department of Finance, for examination, as a distinct reflection upon the Minister of National Defence compared with his colleagues. For that reason, anxious as I am to see this legislation made as tight as it possibly can be to effect the purpose aimed at, I would not be prepared to support an amendment which would have the effect I have mentioned.
I believe the present Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) is quite as capable of seeing that all contracts in his department are just as honourably awarded, and business in that department as well carried out, as other ministers of the crown are with respect to their departments. Under the statute mentioned by the Minister of Pensions and National Health there is a provision that wherever contracts are in excess of $5,000, public tenders must be called for. The amount of $5,000 was fixed in this particular legislation with that precedent in mind, and I think it is a pretty fair basis to go on. I do submit that this legislation is a departure, going a long way in a new direction, and the effort
Defence Purchasing Board

we are making in the matter would, I believe, only be impeded in the long run if at this stage we tried to go further along the road of change than we are going in the bill which is now before us. I am sure the leader of the opposition has the same purpose we have in seeking to make this measure as acceptable as possible to the public; but having had a good deal to do with the administration of large departments, he knows that there are many matters that do not appear on the face of things when legislation is being put through, which come to play an important part later on in administration. If after this measure is on the statutes and its efficacy tested it is found that there is some special reason why contracts of a smaller amount should go before the board, that will be time enough to consider the question; but for the present we are, I believe, going far enough if we retain the figure now proposed.

May I say this, in regard to war records. My hon. friend has referred to this matter. Since the war I have been before the Canadian people in five general elections, and on four occasions out of five I have been returned as Prime Minister of this country. That is the answer.

speechtext: I rise to a question of privilege. The leader of the opposition has spread on the record the statement that I had remained at home and had refused to enlist.

subtopic: CREATION OP DEFENCE PURCHASING BOARD TO ENTER INTO CONTRACTS FOR MUNITIONS, EQUIPMENT, MATERIALS AND SUPPLIES

subtopic: CREATION OP DEFENCE PURCHASING BOARD TO ENTER INTO CONTRACTS FOR MUNITIONS, EQUIPMENT, MATERIALS AND SUPPLIES
speechtext: The hon. member said, at any rate, that I had remained at home while he was at war. On a question of privilege I wish to say that on August 4, 1914, with the regiment to which I belong, I was summoned to take the field at Fort La Martiniere, where we were - in service until December, 1914. Since then for three times I enlisted in the Canadian expeditionary force. The regiments in which I was were disbanded, were sent as drafts, and we were left behind. The only question that arises is that I was not jin London, as so many others, who for months and months were waiting for appointments to the front, and were returned to Canada. My record can be compared with that of any other.
